issue:
Expose import.incremental_skip_later config option as CLI option
To reduce the time needed for manual prompting during the import of a large number of tracks and to import as much as possible without prompting, I run the import once with the `-i --quiet` options and the `import.incremental_skip_later` config option enabled and then again without the `--quiet` option and `import.incremental_skip_later` disabled within the configuration, letting beets prompt for the previously skipped tracks only.
However, currently that requires me to change the configuration file during the workflow which I'd like to avoid.
<!--
If you're landing here as a user, we ask you bring up your idea in the
Discussions (https://github.com/beetbox/beets/discussions).
-->

### Proposed solution

In addition to the configuration file the  `import.incremental_skip_later` option should be configurable via the CLI as e.g. `--incremental-skip-later` option of the `import` command.

Usage example:
```sh
beet import -siq --incremental-skip-later # no questions asked, tracks skipped in doubt
beet import -si                           # prompting for previously skipped tracks only
```

### Objective

<!-- Ref to Discussions -->

#### Goals

<!-- What is the purpose of feature request? -->
Improving the import workflow / making the import command more flexible.

#### Non-goals

<!--
What else could be accomplished with this feature request, but is currently out
of scope?
-->
Changing the import behaviour internally.

#### Anti-goals

<!--
What could go wrong (side effects) if we implement this feature request?
-->
Any additional complexity or more prompts. :smile:

kel.goal: Allow importing music files directly from a previous import logfile
kel.desc:
Allow importing from logfile
When importing large collections, it makes sense to do the automated import first, then do the manual part afterwards:

    $ beet import -l skipped.log -q /path/to/library

It would be great if it was possible to continue the import using the logfile instead of a directory:

    $ beet import skipped.log

Beets should be able to parse the logfile and call import on each directory that was skipped.
kel.procedure: importing skipped files directly from a previous import logfile
steps: Examine the CLI import command parser and execution logic to see how import log files are created and how file paths are validated and gathered.
Add a `--from-logfile` option to the import command parser allowing multiple log files to be supplied.

Implement a helper to parse logfiles line by line, validating line formats and verbs ('asis', 'skip', 'duplicate-skip' vs ignored verbs like 'import', 'duplicate-keep', 'duplicate-replace'), extracting path components with commonpath.

Integrate logfile path extraction into the import command handler, ensuring missing user-specified paths raise UserError while missing logfile paths produce warnings, raising UserError only if no valid paths remain.
Run unit tests verifying valid and invalid logfile line parsing, skipped path extraction, and handling of non-existent log paths.
pitfalls: Do not fail immediately if a path read from a logfile does not exist on disk; log a warning instead, as files might have been moved or imported elsewhere.
Do not import paths marked with completed action verbs like 'import' or 'duplicate-keep'.
Ensure semicolon-separated file paths on a single log line are reduced to their common ancestor directory before importing.

@@ -79,6 +79,43 @@ def _do_query(lib, query, album, also_items=True):
     return items, albums
 
 
+def _paths_from_logfile(path):
+    """Parse the logfile and yield skipped paths to pass to the `import`
+    command.
+    """
+    with open(path, mode="r", encoding="utf-8") as fp:
+        for i, line in enumerate(fp, start=1):
+            verb, sep, paths = line.rstrip("\n").partition(" ")
+            if not sep:
+                raise ValueError(f"line {i} is invalid")
+
+            # Ignore informational lines that don't need to be re-imported.
+            if verb in {"import", "duplicate-keep", "duplicate-replace"}:
+                continue
+
+            if verb not in {"asis", "skip", "duplicate-skip"}:
+                raise ValueError(f"line {i} contains unknown verb {verb}")
+
+            yield os.path.commonpath(paths.split("; "))
+
+
+def _parse_logfiles(logfiles):
+    """Parse all `logfiles` and yield paths from it."""
+    for logfile in logfiles:
+        try:
+            yield from _paths_from_logfile(syspath(normpath(logfile)))
+        except ValueError as err:
+            raise ui.UserError('malformed logfile {}: {}'.format(
+                util.displayable_path(logfile),
+                str(err)
+            )) from err
+        except IOError as err:
+            raise ui.UserError('unreadable logfile {}: {}'.format(
+                util.displayable_path(logfile),
+                str(err)
+            )) from err

kel.desc:
scrub: The `auto` option should be a no-op when `import.write` is disabled
### Problem

I was importing new tracks with `import.write` disabled and seeing all tracks populated with new tags. With help from the [forum](https://discourse.beets.io/t/tags-are-being-written-to-imported-files-even-though-import-write-no/2068/4), I was able to determine that with `scrub.auto` enabled and `import.write` disabled, the scrub plugin removes tags and rewrites them from the database.
The [scrub documentation](https://beets.readthedocs.io/en/stable/plugins/scrub.html#automatic-scrubbing) indicates that s
kel.procedure: Bypass automatic file scrubbing during import when write disabled
steps: Inspect the scrub plugin's import event listener to determine how `scrub.auto` interacts with the `import.write` setting.
Update the auto-scrub hook logic triggered on import to check if writing is enabled, returning early as a no-op when `import.write` is False.
Run importer tests to confirm that tags are not stripped and rewritten during import when write is disabled.
pitfalls: Do not scrub files when `import.write` is false, as scrubbing deletes tags from the audio file and cannot re-write database tags without writing being enabled.
Do not confuse standalone scrubbing commands (manual `beet scrub`) with the automatic import hook.

kel.desc:
Selection interface: option to "skip remaining tracks" and take action
### Problem

I love the `modify` command's select mode, because it means you don't have to write super-specific queries - instead you can write a more general query and then simply type an `n` to skip those tracks you don't want to retag.

Unfortunately, there seems to be no way to "skip remaining tracks". For example, say I got through 50 out of 100 tracks that a query returned. I've answered `y` to most of them, but `n` to just a few. If I hit Ctrl-C at this point, I notice that the tags do not get written to the trac

Handle the 'q' option by immediately returning the already-accumulated list of selected objects rather than aborting or prompting remaining items.

issue:
Proposed check: don't allow argument unpacking in a call after a keyword argument
Imagine a function like

```py
def foo(bar, baz):
    pass
```

The following call is a syntactically incorrect:

```py
foo(baz="baz", "bar")
```

However, with unpacking the following is allowed:

```py
foo(baz="baz", *["bar"])
```

[However](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/82741#issuecomment-1093845041),

> [T]he resulting argument binding is awkward, and almost never does what you want/expect it to

It was [not ruled a bug or a behavior that can or should be deprecated](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/82741#issuecomment-1093845049). Still, I think in most cases this is probably an oversight and should not be used.

If we want this check, I would be willing to contribute a patch.

 This check identifies exception types that are specified in multiple ``except``

+**B026**: Star-arg unpacking after a keyword argument is strongly discouraged, because
+it only works when the keyword parameter is declared after all parameters supplied by

+There was `cpython discussion of disallowing this syntax
+<https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/82741>`_, but legacy usage and parser
+limitations make it difficult.

kel.desc:
[BUG] nan singular vectors in `tl.partial_svd`
Occasionally `tl.partial_svd` returns nans when `max_dim > n_eigenvecs > rank`.
```python3
import tensorly as tl
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(1)

a = tl.dot(tl.randn((4, 2)), tl.randn((2, 4)))
u, s, v = tl.partial_svd(a, n_eigenvecs=3)
print(u)

kel.goal: Support exporting two-dimensional datasets to raster format
kel.desc:
Add support for `to_raster()` with 2D datasets.
It is often times useful to write a dataset to a raster. This is only possible if the data is 2D as the band dimension is taken by the different variables.

It would be nice to support metadata and writing band descriptions.
kel.procedure: Exporting 2D xarray datasets to multi-band raster files
steps: Inspect the existing `to_raster` implementation for DataArray objects on the raster accessor and identify the corresponding Dataset accessor class.
Implement `to_raster` on `RasterDataset` ensuring the dataset variables are verified as 2D spatial arrays sharing coordinates, CRS, and transform.

Handle dataset-to-raster writing by treating each data variable as a raster band, setting band descriptions to variable names, preserving or homogenizing nodata/metadata, and passing rasterio creation options.
Handle mismatch cases gracefully, such as validating consistent dimensions or rejecting variables with mismatched nodata when writing to formats requiring a single global nodata.
Run the integration tests for exporting datasets to raster.
pitfalls: Assuming all variables can have distinct nodata values when writing to raster formats like GeoTIFF that only store a single dataset-level nodata value.
Allowing non-2D variables (or variables without spatial dimensions) to be treated as bands without validation or filtering.
Failing to set band descriptions from dataset variable names when converting dataset variables to raster bands.

kel.goal: Preserve cursor position when focusing the Input widget
kel.desc:
Focusing Input widget should not move cursor to the end
When the Input widget is focused, the cursor currently moves to the end.

This leads to a flickering effect when it's focused via a click, as the cursor jumps to the end (due to the focus handler), and then jumps to the click location (due to the click handler).

**Desired behaviour:** When the Input is focused via keyboard, the cursor moves back to the position it was previously at the last time it was focused. When focused via click, it goes directly to the click location without jumping to the end first.
kel.procedure: preserve input cursor position on widget focus
steps: Inspect the widget's focus handler and cursor position initialization logic to identify where cursor position is forced to the end of the input value on focus.
Remove the line in `_on_focus` that overrides `cursor_position` to `len(self.value)`, ensuring the cursor retains its existing position when focused.
Introduce a state flag (e.g. `_initial_value = True`) so that the cursor position is placed at the end only during the initial value assignment in `_watch_value`.
Refactor cursor blinking logic into helper methods (`_restart_blink_cycle` and `_pause_blink_cycle`) and hook them into focus, blur, key, and mouse events.
Run the input modification test suite to verify that key actions and cursor positioning behave correctly.
pitfalls: Resetting cursor position to the end of the text unconditionally in the focus event handler causes visual flicker on mouse clicks and loses user cursor position on keyboard navigation.
Failing to set initial cursor position when the widget is created with an initial value leaves the cursor at index 0 rather than the end of the initial text.

issue:
Support additional configuration parameters for S3 transfer
**Problem**
When using S3 as remote for DVC, boto3 reads also the configuration file `~/.aws/config` typically used by the original AWS CLI tool. Not all configuration parameters from this file have an effect in DVC at the moment. For instance, the last line `multipart_threshold = 500MB` will be skipped by DVC while the previous line `signature_version = s3` will be applied when pushing data into S3:      
```ini
[default]
output = json
s3 =
  signature_version = s3
  multipart_threshold = 500MB
```
**Suggestion**
Suggestion is to support optional yet useful parameters from `~/.aws/config` as per [AWS CLI S3 documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/topic/s3-config.html) to control S3 transfers for performance reasons or to unlock the advanced configuration capabilities. 

These parameters should be passed to TransferConfig:
- `max_concurrent_requests` - The maximum number of concurrent requests.
- `max_queue_size` - The maximum number of tasks in the task queue.
- `multipart_threshold` - The size threshold the CLI uses for multipart transfers of individual files.
- `multipart_chunksize` - When using multipart transfers, this is the chunk size that the CLI uses for multipart transfers of individual files.
- `max_bandwidth` - The maximum bandwidth that will be consumed for uploading and downloading data to and from Amazon S3.

If it is reasonable and doable - support also the following set of parameters:
- `use_accelerate_endpoint` - Use the Amazon S3 Accelerate endpoint for all s3 and s3api commands. You must first enable S3 Accelerate on your bucket before attempting to use the endpoint. This is mutually exclusive with the use_dualstack_endpoint option.
- `use_dualstack_endpoint` - Use the Amazon S3 dual IPv4 / IPv6 endpoint for all s3 and s3api commands. This is mutually exclusive with the use_accelerate_endpoint option.
- `addressing_style` - Specifies which addressing style to use. This controls if the bucket name is in the hostname or part of the URL. Value values are: path, virtual, and auto. The default value is auto.
- `payload_signing_enabled` - Refers to whether or not to SHA256 sign sigv4 payloads. By default, this is disabled for streaming uploads (UploadPart and PutObject) when using https.

These values must be set under the top level `s3` key in the AWS Config File, which has a default location of `~/.aws/config`. Below is an example configuration:
```ini
[profile development]
aws_access_key_id=foo
aws_secret_access_key=bar
s3 =
  max_concurrent_requests = 20
  max_queue_size = 10000
  multipart_threshold = 64MB
  multipart_chunksize = 16MB
  max_bandwidth = 50MB/s
  use_accelerate_endpoint = true
  addressing_style = path
```

+    "gb": 1024 ** 3,
+    "tb": 1024 ** 4,
+    "kib": 1024,
+    "mib": 1024 ** 2,
+    "gib": 1024 ** 3,
+    "tib": 1024 ** 4,
+}
+
+
+def human_readable_to_bytes(value):
+    value = value.lower()
+    suffix = None
+    if value.endswith(tuple(MULTIPLIERS.keys())):
+        size = 2
+        size += value[-2] == "i"  # KiB, MiB etc
+        value, suffix = value[:-size], value[-size:]
+
+    multiplier = MULTIPLIERS.get(suffix, 1)
+    return int(value) * multiplier

issue:
Add retries for heartbeats (MRP)
**What feature would you like?**
When a heartbeat fails, an error is logged and the connection is closed. Generally this is good, but in case the response happens to be delayed long enough (even though nothing is wrong), this is quite pessimistic and it's probably a good idea to make another try before failing. Do not impose an initial delay on the retry though (just retry immediately) as we still want to fail as early as possible in case of an actual problem.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
From the description above: make a retry immediately when a heartbeat fails. Only log error if retry also fails.

**Any other information to share?**
Heartbeat errors seems to happen sporadically and I believe there's not actually a problem in most cases. This is an attempt to recover in those cases, but it's still not a very well tested method so I can't be sure that it works.

+HEARTBEAT_RETRIES = 1  # One regular attempt + retries

 OutstandingMessage = namedtuple("OutstandingMessage", "semaphore response")
@@ -23,10 +24,14 @@ async def heartbeat_loop(protocol):
     """Periodically send heartbeat messages to device."""
     _LOGGER.debug("Starting heartbeat loop")
     count = 0
+    attempts = 0
     message = messages.create(protobuf.ProtocolMessage.SEND_COMMAND_MESSAGE)
     while True:
         try:
-            await asyncio.sleep(HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL)
+            # Re-attempts are made with no initial delay to more quickly
+            # recover a failed heartbeat (if possible)
+            if attempts == 0:
+                await asyncio.sleep(HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL)
 
             _LOGGER.debug("Sending periodic heartbeat %d", count)
             await protocol.send_and_receive(message)
@@ -34,11 +39,18 @@ async def heartbeat_loop(protocol):
         except asyncio.CancelledError:
             break

-            _LOGGER.exception(f"heartbeat {count} failed")
-            protocol.connection.close()
-            break
+            attempts += 1
+            if attempts > HEARTBEAT_RETRIES:
+                _LOGGER.error(f"heartbeat {count} failed after {attempts} tries")
+                protocol.connection.close()
+                break
+            else:
+                _LOGGER.debug(f"heartbeat {count} failed")

+            attempts = 0

kel.goal: Fix multiline export sorting corruption with sort reexports option
kel.desc:
BUG: --sort-reexports don't work with multiple lines __all__
```python
import datetime

from mylib import (
    module1,
    module2,
    module3,
    module4,
)

__all__ = (
    "func1",
    "func2",
    "func3",
    "func4",
)
```

after using `isort file.py --sort-reexports`, becomes:
```python
import datetime

fro__all__ = ('func1', 'func2', 'func3', 'func4')
```
It seems to me that there is a problem with calculating the current index when using reexports in cases where we use multiline exports or add comments _to the beginning of the file_.
kel.procedure: relative stream seek and truncate for reexport rewriting
steps: Identify where reexported literal definitions like `__all__` are parsed and rewritten to the output stream.
Reproduce the corruption when running with `--sort-reexports` on multiline imports and exports.
Replace absolute character tracking (`sort_section_pointer`) with relative rollback tracking (`reexport_rollback`) based on the length of the line where reexport sorting started.

When rewriting the sorted code for a reexport, seek back by `output_stream.tell() - reexport_rollback`, reset rollback to 0, write the sorted code, and call `output_stream.truncate()` to remove any remaining stale output.
Verify that multiline imports and exports are sorted and output cleanly without overwriting earlier lines.
pitfalls: Using an accumulator for absolute stream position easily desynchronizes when previous sections are rewritten or multiline imports expand/contract.
Failing to call `output_stream.truncate()` after seeking and overwriting can leave trailing garbage characters if the newly formatted code is shorter than what was previously buffered.

In some cases, users need a direct link to a data file in the cloud. It might be just a matter of convenience or when DVC is used from automation tools like CD4ML scenarios. We need to provide a way to get a direct link.

I suggest creating a new command `dvc resolve`. Other options can be also be considered. For example, it might be a part of `dvc status` (when it start supporting data files as argument).

$ dvc resolve file.txt df.csv --rev ada9d973
file.txt s3://dvc-temp/dataset1/d30abac6950583e6a5f1dcd31cb1043b
df.csv gs://project42/cache/2290babda371e52eeca2a2065a358783

kel.goal: Optimize pull performance when specifying multiple target files
kel.desc:
Pull with masked targets is slow
`dvc pull` with specifying targets by shell-expanded glob mask (e.g. `dvc pull */*.dvc`) works significantly slower then global `dvc pull`. This is especially hurtful when pulling large number of small files. At the same time, passing glob mask to dvc via `dvc pull '*/*.dvc'` does not seem to be supported.

Should this be optimized?

As mentioned in chat, workaround is `dvc pull -R dir`.

DVC version: 0.50.1
Platform: Ubuntu 18.04, installation via pip
kel.procedure: batch multi-target data sync operations instead of looping per target
steps: Identify where data sync commands (pull, push, fetch, status) iterate over targets sequentially at the CLI command level.
Refactor CLI command handlers to pass all targets at once (`targets=self.args.targets`) instead of executing `do_run(target)` in a loop.
Update underlying repository API methods (`pull`, `push`, `fetch`, `status`, `used_cache`, `_local_status`, `_cloud_status`) to accept `targets` as a collection instead of a single `target`.
Aggregate stages for all specified targets during cache collection in `used_cache` and `status` so remote/local sync runs in a single batch operation.
Run test suite to verify data sync operations across multiple targets.
pitfalls: Performing network fetch/push inside a loop over individual targets prevents batching and connection reuse across target files.
Forgetting to iterate over targets during checkout stage when `pull` completes might skip local file checkout for multiple targets.

kel.goal: Support pulling specific targets when using run cache
kel.desc:
Make `dvc pull --run-cache` allow `targets` for a granular pull process
Right now, if I do 

`dvc pull [target]`
this will pull *only* the `target` I am interested in.

However, if I do `dvc pull --run-cache [targets]`
the `target` is ignored, *everything* is pulled from remote. Not even a warning is thrown that `--run-cache` does not accept granularly pulling files.


This is based on https://discuss.dvc.org/t/dvc-pull-run-cache-target/444 discussion
kel.procedure: respect target filters when fetching run cache and add pull support on restore
steps: Locate fetch logic and stage run cache restoration handling target filtering and stage execution.
Remove unconstrained run-cache pulling during target-filtered fetch calls so targets are respected when collecting used cache.
Pass a `--pull` argument through `repro` command options down to stage restoration to pull missing run-cache stage outputs on demand.
Verify the command argument defaults and parsing by running repro unit tests.
pitfalls: Pulling the whole run cache inside fetch before filtering targets causes all objects to be retrieved regardless of target parameters.
Forgetting to pass keyword arguments (`**kwargs`) through stage `run` and `run_stage` functions prevents `--pull` from reaching `stage_cache.restore`.

These files were all created in the `logs` directory.

kel.goal: Recommend single-dimension and hybrid modes when validation errors occur
kel.desc:
Recommend re-running in hybrid/single mode when errors found in batch mode
When spectacles is run in batch mode and encounters an error, we should suggest the user re-run the explore (maybe even pre-populating the command with the explore argument in the output) in single-dimension mode to zero in on the dimensions causing the error.

Here's a suggested output:

```
To determine the exact dimensions responsible for this error, you can re-run this explore in single-dimension mode.

You can also run this original validation with `--mode hybrid` to do this automatically.
```
kel.procedure: Recommend alternative validation modes on batch error
steps: Identify the code path responsible for reporting validation results and errors in batch mode. The recommendation message should be displayed after individual error details but before the final error exit.

Implement properties on `Explore`, `Model`, and `Project` classes to recursively count the total number of validation errors. This count is needed to dynamically phrase the recommendation message (e.g., 'this error' vs. 'these errors').

Add a conditional log message in the `run_sql` function in `spectacles/cli.py`. This message should only appear when the validation `mode` is 'batch' and errors have occurred. The message should recommend re-running in single-dimension mode (`--mode single`) or hybrid mode (`--mode hybrid`), using the newly implemented error count to correctly pluralize 'error'.
Run the provided tests to ensure the error counting logic and the overall behavior are correct.
pitfalls: Hardcoding the recommendation message without considering the number of errors, leading to incorrect grammar (e.g., 'this errors').
Placing the recommendation message in a location where it would always be displayed, even if no errors occurred or if not in batch mode.
Incorrectly calculating the total number of errors across nested LookML objects, leading to an inaccurate count for the recommendation message.

issue:
Should marshmallow helpers respect `only`, `exclude`?
When introspecting `Nested` fields, we don't check for the `only` or `exclude` attributes. For example:

``` python
class FooSchema(Schema):
    bar = fields.Str()
    baz = fields.Str()

class BobSchema(Schema):
    foo = fields.Nested(FooSchema, only=('bar', ))
```

If we call `schema2jsonschema(BobSchema)`, the nested `foo` will include `bar` and `baz` fields, even though `baz` will never be included in this case. Which isn't necessarily a problem, unless `baz` is required:

``` python
class FooSchema(Schema):
    bar = fields.Str()
    baz = fields.Str(required=True)
```

In this case, users of apispec will likely return JSON that wouldn't validate against the definition schema, since there's going to be a missing required field. I haven't actually encountered this situation, and I don't know how often it's going to come up--just wanted to raise for discussion.

The [PEP 513 whitelist](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0513/#the-manylinux1-policy) includes `libpanelw.so.5` and `libncursesw.so.5`, both of which are part of ncurses version 5.

I'm told that Fedora 24 and successors have already switched to ncurses 6, with the ncurses 5 libraries being available in a compatibility package, but not installed by default. So... I guess these have to be dropped from the whitelist.

SNOW-1013234: Fix config permissions warning message 
### What is the current behavior?

If permissions / owner of config file is incorrect, the command outputs long one-liner containing two commands (`chmod` and `chown`) to call to fix the issue.
1. Many users tend to overlook that there are two commands and give up after one does not fix the issue
2. In Snowflake CLI on MacOS default config path is inside "Application Support" directory - space inside the path turned out to be problematic for some users

```
/Users/pczajka/Snowflake/venv3.12/lib/python3.12/site-packages/snowflake/connector/config_manager.py:344: UserWarning: Bad owner or permissions on /Users/pczajka/Library/Application Support/snowflake/config.toml. To change owner, run `chown $USER /Users/pczajka/Library/Application Support/snowflake/config.toml`. To restrict permissions, run `chmod 0600 /Users/pczajka/Library/Application Support/snowflake/config.toml`.
  warn(f"Bad owner or permissions on {str(filep)}{chmod_message}")
  ```

### What is the desired behavior?

Reformattinmg the message to highlight that there are two commands to call (fix 1) and add quotes around filenames (fix 2).
For example:
```
/Users/pczajka/Snowflake/venv3.12/lib/python3.12/site-packages/snowflake/connector/config_manager.py:344: UserWarning: Bad owner or permissions on /Users/pczajka/Library/Application Support/snowflake/config.toml.
 * To change owner, run `chown $USER "/Users/pczajka/Library/Application Support/snowflake/config.toml"`.
 * To restrict permissions, run `chmod 0600 "/Users/pczajka/Library/Application Support/snowflake/config.toml"`.
  warn(f"Bad owner or permissions on {str(filep)}{chmod_message}")
  ```

### How would this improve `snowflake-connector-python`?

Improve user experience (also improve user experience of Snowflake CLI)

### References and other background

_No response_

kel.procedure: thread-safe file cache pickle operations under mutex lock
steps: Locate cache class file and identify unsafe non-thread-safe dictionary access during serialization/deserialization or lookup in multi-threaded file cache.
Reproduce thread safety or segmentation fault issues when multiple threads access and serialize cache entries simultaneously.

issue:
Should we somehow expose Pipe*Stream on Unix, and if so, how?
We have `PipeReceiveStream` and `PipeSendStream` classes on Unix, that are currently not exposed publicly; they're only used internally for subprocesses.

The actual code is a pretty generic building block: they can wrap around any Unix file-descriptor that supports non-blocking mode. So they could potentially be useful for talking to [FIFOs](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/fifo.7.html), TTYs, stdio streams (#174), etc.

Should we expose them more directly? If so, how? In `trio.hazmat`, with some sort of [`os.fdopen`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.fdopen) equivalent?

If we do we'll want to think through the ownership semantics: should they take ownership of a passed in fd, or should they dup it?

Also, they should restore the fd's blocking/non-blocking state before closing it.

Maybe move_on_after(0)/fail_after(0) should immediately cancel their scope

```python

        await self.accept()
```

kel.procedure: Ensure immediate cancellation for already-expired cancel scopes
steps: Understand that `move_on_after(0)` or `fail_after(0)` scopes do not immediately cancel due to the timing of timeout processing in the event loop. This can lead to non-blocking operations succeeding before cancellation is applied.
Locate the `CancelScope` class definition in `trio/_core/_run.py`, as this is where the core logic for managing cancellation scopes resides.

Modify the `CancelScope.__enter__` method to check if the scope's deadline is already in the past at the moment of entry. If `current_time()` is greater than or equal to `self._deadline`, immediately set `self.cancel_called = True` to mark the scope as cancelled.
Verify that the fix correctly implements immediate cancellation for zero-timeout scopes and does not introduce regressions.
pitfalls: Assuming that `move_on_after(0)` or `fail_after(0)` will always cancel before any operation within their scope can execute, without understanding Trio's event loop scheduling.
Attempting to implement a 'check once, but don't block' semantic using `move_on_after(0)` or `fail_after(0)` without this fix, as the behavior would be accidental and unreliable.

kel.goal: Parse FTP directory listing dates with single-space separators
kel.desc:
`parse_ls_date` doesn't handle singe-spaced servers.
I'm using aioftp across a multitude of FTP servers, and just discovered that one of them uses a timestamp of `%b %d %Y` instead of `%b %d  %Y`.
Because the parser assumes the date is exactly 12 characters long, it will catch `Jan 03 2018` as `Jan 03 2018 `. This in turn leads to a datetime parsing error.
kel.procedure: strip ls date strings before datetime parsing
steps: Locate where FTP directory listing lines are parsed into file metadata and where `parse_ls_date` is called.
Apply `.strip()` on the sliced date string (`s[:12].strip()`) before passing it to `parse_ls_date` to remove trailing spaces from single-spaced date formats.
Run the test suite including directory listing parsing tests to confirm both double-spaced and single-spaced dates parse successfully.
pitfalls: Changing the slicing boundary from 12 characters instead of stripping whitespace can break parsing for standard 12-character format dates like 'Nov 18  1958' or 'Nov 18 12:29'.

kel.procedure: Implement dynamic programming for longest common subsequence

pitfalls: Forgetting to add the new function to `__all__` in `__init__.py`, making it inaccessible via `from pythainlp.util import ...`.

+.. _setting_a_seed:
+
+Setting a random seed
+=====================
+
+The library has a variety of strategies whose behaviour is stochastic. To ensure
+reproducible results a random seed should be set. As both Numpy and the standard
+library are used for random number generation, both seeds need to be
+set. To do this we can use the `seed` function::
+
+    >>> import axelrod as axl
+    >>> players = (axl.Random(), axl.MetaMixer())  # Two stochastic strategies
+    >>> axl.seed(0)
+    >>> axl.Match(players, turns=3).play()
+    [('D', 'C'), ('D', 'D'), ('C', 'D')]
+
+We obtain the same results is it is played with the same seed::
+
+    >>> axl.seed(0)
+    >>> axl.Match(players, turns=3).play()
+    [('D', 'C'), ('D', 'D'), ('C', 'D')]
+
+Note that this is equivalent to::
+
+    >>> import numpy
+    >>> import random
+    >>> players = (axl.Random(), axl.MetaMixer())
+    >>> random.seed(0)
+    >>> numpy.random.seed(0)
+    >>> axl.Match(players, turns=3).play()
+    [('D', 'C'), ('D', 'D'), ('C', 'D')]
+    >>> numpy.random.seed(0)
+    >>> random.seed(0)
+    >>> axl.Match(players, turns=3).play()
+    [('D', 'C'), ('D', 'D'), ('C', 'D')]

kel.procedure: filter strategy classes by classifier dictionary attributes
steps: Examine how strategies and their `classifier` dictionaries are structured and exposed in the strategies module.

Create helper filter functions (`passes_operator_filter`, `passes_in_list_filter`, and `passes_filterset`) that inspect strategy classifiers, normalize special values like string `'infinity'` to `float('inf')`, support equality/comparison operators, and verify subset conditions for list attributes like `makes_use_of`.
Map supported filter keys (e.g., boolean flags, exact memory depth, `min_memory_depth`, `max_memory_depth`, and `makes_use_of`) to corresponding filter predicates in `passes_filterset`.

pitfalls: Failing to convert string representations like `'infinity'` to `float('inf')` will cause inequality comparisons on `memory_depth` to raise `TypeError` or fail in Python 3.

Create filesystem tree abstractions (such as working tree vs git object tree wrappers) providing unified open/walk/isdir/exists methods for a given revision.
Update commands and utilities (like metrics reading, walking files, and brancher) to query the tree abstraction for a given target revision instead of invoking git checkout.
Run test suite to verify commands inspect historical/branch revisions cleanly without workspace side-effects.
pitfalls: Relying on working directory paths or OS file system functions directly when traversing historic revisions.
Failing to handle uncommitted workspace changes when iteration includes both working tree state and git revisions.

issue:
Discontinue (direct) usage of any runner implementations
With #538 we made the start of a new paradigm: iterator-based interaction with (concurrent) subprocesses.

It is our (@mih and @christian-monch) understanding that this basic approach would work for most (if not all) use cases that involve the execution of subprocesses. Respective experiments have been made and the results look promising. The "ultimate" challenge will be the implementation of a queue-based remote shell.

In order to bring down the complexity of implementations after the introduction of this new paradigm, all subprocess execution in datalad-next should be switch to it.

Afterwards all runner-related imports from datalad-core should be discontinued (which involves updating any extensions that make use of it).

This plan answers the questions of #519. `GitRunner` has no future.

kel.goal: Consolidate filesystem directory traversers into a shared layered implementation
kel.desc:
Consolidate "traverser" from gooey and metalad into a common implementation
This implementation should be layered, to be useful for listing, but also status/diff reporting.

It should also be benchmarked, relative to git-lsdir and and git-ls-tree.

Ping @christian-monch
kel.procedure: implementing layered git traversal and structured status results
steps: Identify the existing filesystem and git traversal abstractions needing consolidation and plan a layered design separating raw git subprocess execution, diff/status iterators, and command-level result reporting.
Create a unified result reporting hierarchy using dataclasses (`CommandResult` and command-specific subclasses like `StatusResult`) supporting dict-like access for legacy result handlers.
Implement low-level git command runners and layered iterators (such as `iter_gitstatus` and `iter_gitdiff`) to stream structured git state items.
Implement the status command interface consuming the layered git iterators, mapping git diff and tree item states into structured command results.
Register the new status command into the command suite.
Execute unit tests covering git runners, diff/status iterators, and command result data models.
pitfalls: Using `@dataclass(kw_only=True)` when maintaining compatibility with Python versions prior to 3.10 causes a TypeError on subclassing.
Failing to provide dict-like accessors (`__getitem__`, `get`, `items`) on `CommandResult` breaks legacy DataLad result processing loops expecting dict records.

kel.goal: Implement non-in-place bitwise or operation for AltConstraints
kel.desc:
Implement `AltConstraints.__or__` not `__ior__`
This is the sibling of https://github.com/datalad/datalad/issues/7164.

I think the real issue is that the current implementation matches the semantics of `__ior__()` and not `__or__()`.

And this needs to be fixed.

Breaking backward compatibility when renaming classes by not maintaining aliases for the old class names.

kel.goal: Standardize and document item name path conventions for collection iterators
kel.desc:
Double check and document (if needed) `.name` conventions for `iter_collections`
I cannot put my finger on it, but I feel the nature of the value of `.name` for a reported item is non-uniform.

I am not aware of a documentation for the convention, if how iterators should behave.

The `.name` should always be a `PurePath|Path` objects.

However, should it carry the base path (key argument to the iterator) in it? Or not?

It would make sense to me to never have it. Rational:

There is no reason while a (file) collection should be on a file system. It could have a very non-Path base add
kel.procedure: standardizing collection iterator item name types and path properties
steps: Inspect the base item classes and collection iterator item dataclasses to identify discrepancies between raw string identifiers (such as archive members or git paths) and PurePath/Path instances.
Update PathBasedItem in iter_collections/utils.py to define a cached_property `path` returning PurePath(self.name), and FileSystemItem to provide a cached_property `link_target_path`.
Update format-specific items like TarfileItem and GitTreeItem to store `name` (and `link_target`) as raw `str` and provide cached properties returning PurePosixPath instances.
Ensure worktree items override `name` as `PurePath` and update yield docstrings across iterators (annexworktree, directory, gittree, gitworktree, tarfile) documenting their path and name conventions.
Run collection iterator and ls file collection test suites to verify that item name conventions and path properties function properly across archive and git formats.
pitfalls: Forcing `name` to always be a PurePath or Path breaks POSIX-specific collection formats (such as tar or git trees) on non-POSIX operating systems where certain characters or separators are invalid.
Do not remove the `name` attribute or change its type without providing cached `path` properties for consumers that require PurePath instances.

kel.goal: Add a command-line tool to run sed replacements across repositories
kel.desc:
Make an `all-repos-sed`
Sometimes I don't want to write the full gamut of a fixer and such and really just want some nice `sed -i`.

I think the interface would be something like:

```
$ all-repos-sed 's/foo/bar/g' -- baz.f
```

And this tool would make a fixer which does essentially (for each repository):

```
git ls-files -- baz.f | xargs sed -i 's/foo/bar/g'
```
kel.procedure: Add git-aware sed autofix CLI tool
steps: Create a helper function for splitting null-byte-delimited bytes output from git ls-files into lists, safely returning an empty list on empty inputs.
Update existing ls-files logic to use the new null-splitting helper instead of inline splitting.

Implement the sed CLI module using autofix infrastructure: define find_repos to filter repositories containing matching files via `git ls-files`, apply_fix to run `sed -i` on matched files, construct default commit messages with shell-quoted commands, and handle CLI arguments including pattern, filename glob, and extended regex.
Register the new CLI executable entry point in setup packaging configuration.
Run test suite to verify the sed fixer and null-split utility function across matching repositories.
pitfalls: Directly calling `bs.rstrip(b'\0').split(b'\0')` on empty bytes returns `[b'']` instead of an empty list `[]`, causing commands to run against an empty filename.
Forgetting to pass `-z` / `--null` handling to `git ls-files` can break when paths contain special characters or spaces.
Omitting `check=True` or `stdout=subprocess.PIPE` when filtering repos via `git ls-files` can cause non-zero exits or silent missed repositories.

+import argparse
+import functools
+import os.path
+import shlex
+import subprocess
+
+from all_repos import autofix_lib
+from all_repos import cli
+from all_repos.util import zsplit
+
+
+def find_repos(config, *, ls_files_cmd):
+    for repo in config.get_cloned_repos():
+        repo_dir = os.path.join(config.output_dir, repo)
+        if subprocess.run(
+            ('git', '-C', repo_dir, *ls_files_cmd[1:]),
+            check=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
+        ).stdout:
+            yield repo_dir
+
+
+def apply_fix(*, ls_files_cmd, sed_cmd):
+    filenames = zsplit(subprocess.check_output(ls_files_cmd))
+    filenames = [f.decode() for f in filenames]
+    autofix_lib.run(*sed_cmd, *filenames)
+
+
+def _quote_cmd(cmd):
+    return ' '.join(shlex.quote(arg) for arg in cmd)
+
+
+def main(argv=None):
+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
+    cli.add_fixer_args(parser)
+    parser.add_argument(
+        '-r', '--regexp-extended',
+        action='store_true',
+        help='use extended regular expressions in the script.',
+    )

issue:
[Slurm adapter] Need to specify custom (GRES) flags for sbatch
Some use cases in Slurm can only be covered with Generic Resource ([GRES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)) scheduling. 
One such example is the reservation of scratch disk space:
https://bugs.schedmd.com/show_bug.cgi?id=2549#c9

Since the name of the GRES is completely arbitrary and up to the HPC-site, it is probably best to have a way to pass arbitrary parameters to `sbatch`. The best place (configuration-wise) is likely the `MachineTypeConfiguration`, so it is similar to the `jdl` funcitonality in HTCondor. 

I ma not yet sure if it is better to allow fully arbitrary parameters or have a dedicated `gres` configuration stanza which directly takes the `gres` to reserve. 

Pinging also @wiene

kel.goal: Map Slurm TIMEOUT job state to stopped resource status
kel.desc:
Drones go into `Error` state when a slurm batch job times out
If a slurm batch job runs out of walltime it will report status `TIMEOUT` in `squeue`. This is not properly recognized by tardis which puts the corresponding VM into `Error` state and repeatedly tries to `scancel` the job (which reports success, since from a slurm point of view things are already as they should be). Tardis keeps the VM in `Error` state until `squeue -o -h -t all` stops reporting the job ID (takes approx. 15 minutes in the case I observed). If that happens proper cleanup seems to happen.

A few snippets from a log
kel.procedure: Map Slurm TIMEOUT status to terminal resource status
steps: Locate the Slurm site adapter where raw Slurm batch job state strings (such as RUNNING, STOPPED, SUSPENDED) are translated to internal resource status enum values.
Review existing state translations and unit tests in tests/adapters_t/sites_t/test_slurm.py to identify how unhandled states default to Error.
Add 'TIMEOUT=ResourceStatus.Deleted' (or the appropriate terminal status mapping) to the Slurm status translation mapping dictionary in the SlurmAdapter class.
Add test assertions in the Slurm adapter unit test checking that TIMEOUT translates to ResourceStatus.Deleted.
Run the Slurm adapter test suite to verify the state translation succeeds.
pitfalls: Mapping TIMEOUT to ResourceStatus.Error causes the runner to repeatedly issue cancellation commands (e.g. scancel) on an already finished job until the scheduler drops it from queue listings.
Mapping TIMEOUT to ResourceStatus.Stopped instead of ResourceStatus.Deleted if the framework expects terminated jobs to be marked Deleted.

kel.goal: Expose the current run mode to plugins during build and runtime
kel.desc:
Expose instance of `WebvizRunMode` during build and runtime
Plugins may have code in their` __init__` method which isn't required to run when building portables. E.g. if their are methods called during `__init__` which are also included in `add_webvizstore`, the code will be executed twice during portable build.

For the examples in `webviz-config`, the gain is negligable, but when processing large datasets in `webvizstore`-decorated functions, the difference in build time may be significant.

+def detect_link_type(workdir):
+    """
+    Determine what type of links the filesystem will let us make in the
+    directory ``workdir``.  If symlinks are allowed, returns ``"symlink"``.
+    Otherwise, if hard links are allowed, returns ``"hardlink"``.  Otherwise,
+    returns ``"copy"``.
+    """
+    srcfile = Path(workdir, f".dandi.{os.getpid()}.src")
+    destfile = Path(workdir, f".dandi.{os.getpid()}.dest")
+    try:
+        srcfile.touch()
+        try:
+            os.symlink(srcfile, destfile)
+        except OSError:
+            try:
+                os.link(srcfile, destfile)
+            except OSError:
+                lgr.info(
+                    "Symlink and hardlink tests both failed; setting files_mode='copy'"
+                )
+                return "copy"
+            else:
+                lgr.info(
+                    "Hard link support autodetected; setting files_mode='hardlink'"
+                )
+                return "hardlink"
+        else:
+            lgr.info("Symlink support autodetected; setting files_mode='symlink'")
+            return "symlink"
+    finally:
+        try:
+            destfile.unlink()
+        except FileNotFoundError:
+            pass
+        try:
+            srcfile.unlink()
+        except FileNotFoundError:
+            pass

diff --git a/docs/polymorphism.rst b/docs/polymorphism.rst
index 6a341d7..9d29b96 100644
--- a/docs/polymorphism.rst
+++ b/docs/polymorphism.rst
@@ -6,7 +6,6 @@ Polymorphism
 PynamoDB supports polymorphism through the use of discriminators.
 
 A discriminator is a value that is written to DynamoDB that identifies the python class being stored.
-(Note: currently discriminators are only supported on MapAttribute subclasses; support for model subclasses coming soon.)
 
 Discriminator Attributes
 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
@@ -49,3 +48,32 @@ A class can also be registered manually:
     Discriminator values are written to DynamoDB.
     Changing the value after items have been saved to the database can result in deserialization failures.
     In order to read items with an old discriminator value, the old value must be manually registered.
+
+
+Model Discriminators
+^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+
+Model classes also support polymorphism through the use of discriminators.
+(Note: currently discriminator attributes cannot be used as the hash or range key of a table.)
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    class ParentModel(Model):
+        class Meta:
+            table_name = 'polymorphic_table'
+        id = UnicodeAttribute(hash_key=True)
+        cls = DiscriminatorAttribute()
+
+    class FooModel(ParentModel, discriminator='Foo'):
+        foo = UnicodeAttribute()
+
+    class BarModel(ParentModel, discriminator='Bar'):
+        bar = UnicodeAttribute()
+
+    BarModel(id='Hello', bar='World!').serialize()
+    # {'id': {'S': 'Hello'}, 'cls': {'S': 'Bar'}, 'bar': {'S': 'World!'}}
+.. note::
+
+    Read operations that are performed on a class that has a discriminator value are slightly modified to ensure that only instances of the class are returned.
+    Query and scan operations transparently add a filter condition to ensure that only items with a matching discriminator value are returned.
+    Get and batch get operations will raise a ``ValueError`` if the returned item(s) are not a subclass of the model being read.

Thanks for this nice project, btw!

# Bug Report

## Description

When attempting to push to remote (Google Cloud Storage) using DVC version `2.10.2` and Python version `3.7.11` I encounter the following error:

```console
$ dvc push     
ERROR: unexpected error - unsupported pickle protocol: 5              

Having any troubles? Hit us up at https://dvc.org/support, we are always happy to help!
```

In my tests on python 3.8 this issue does not happen.

### Reproduce

Install DVC version `2.10.2` with Python version `3.7.11` and attempt to push to remote.
kel.procedure: override diskcache disk_pickle_protocol and wrap cache access to handle pickle exceptions gracefully
steps: Locate diskcache Cache usage across the project and identify where pickle protocol mismatches occur (e.g., Python version differences default to higher pickle protocols like protocol 5).

Create a wrapper around diskcache.Cache and diskcache.Disk that defaults 'disk_pickle_protocol' to a broadly compatible level (such as 4) and translates pickle deserialization/protocol errors into a distinct custom exception.
Replace direct diskcache.Cache and diskcache.Index imports with the wrapped Cache class in state and index modules.
Add exception handling in the CLI entry point to catch the custom disk error and display user-friendly instructions on clearing corrupted cache files.
Run unit tests verifying pickle protocol compatibility and error handling for invalid or higher-protocol cache files.
pitfalls: Relying on default diskcache configuration without specifying disk_pickle_protocol defaults to higher pickle versions supported only on newer Python interpreters.
Catching broad ValueError without checking if it contains 'pickle protocol' in the error message, which may swallow unrelated validation errors.

In [Zulip 2.1.0](https://zulip.com/api/changelog#changes-in-zulip-21), the `is_muted` stream subscription property was added and replaced the `in_home_view` property. But the server had still only been sending [subscription update events](https://zulip.com/api/get-events#subscription-update) for the `in_home_view` property when a user muted/unmuted a subscribed stream.

In https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/22695 (API feature level 139), we updated `do_change_subscription_property` so that the server sends a subscription update
kel.procedure: support both inverted legacy and modern boolean properties in event handlers
steps: Identify the event handler processing stream subscription update events and check which property keys it accepts.
Allow both legacy (e.g. `in_home_view`) and new (e.g. `is_muted`) property keys in the event filtering condition.
Normalize the property boolean value, accounting for the opposite boolean polarity between the legacy and new property types.
Add idempotency checks before adding or removing the item from the muted set to avoid duplicate modifications if both events are received.
Run unit tests covering subscription update events for both legacy and new muted property formats.
pitfalls: Failing to invert `in_home_view` when normalizing to `is_muted` state (`in_home_view == True` means unmuted, whereas `is_muted == True` means muted).
Not guarding against duplicate state changes (e.g. attempting to remove from or add to sets without checking existence) when the server sends both legacy and new events for the same action.

+
+
+class dispatches_events:
+    """Decorate function to :func:`.dispatch_event` on entry and exit."""
+
+    def __init__(self, basename):
+        self.before_eventname = 'before_' + basename
+        self.after_eventname = 'after_' + basename
+
+    def __call__(self, fn):
+        if not callable(fn):
+            raise TypeError("decorated object must be callable")
+
+        @wraps(fn)
+        def wrapped(*pargs, **kwargs):
+            sig = inspect.signature(fn)
+            bound = sig.bind(*pargs, **kwargs)
+            bound.apply_defaults()
+            args = bound.arguments
+            obj = args.pop('self', None)
+
+            dispatch_event(self.before_eventname, obj=obj, args=args)
+            try:
+                rval = fn(*pargs, **kwargs)
+            except Exception as exc:
+                dispatch_event(self.after_eventname, obj=obj, args=args, exception=exc)
+                raise
+            else:
+                dispatch_event(self.after_eventname, obj=obj, args=args, return_value=rval)
+                return rval
+
+        return wrapped

kel.goal: Prevent client solver retrieval from mutating default configuration values
kel.desc:
Client.get_solver mutates instance defaults
```
defaults = dict(solver=dict(order_by='id'))

with Client.from_config(defaults=defaults) as client:
    assert 'order_by' in client.defaults['solver']
    solver = client.get_solver()
    assert 'order_by' not in client.defaults['solver']
```
kel.procedure: Prevent configuration mutation by deep-copying default dictionaries before popping keys
steps: Identify where default solver configuration filters are assigned and modified in the client retrieval method.
Reproduce the issue by initializing a client with defaults containing an 'order_by' key in 'solver' and asserting the key is deleted from client.defaults after calling get_solver().
Use copy.deepcopy when falling back to default configuration dictionaries so in-place operations like  dict.pop do not mutate the stored instance defaults.
Ensure that any extra configuration keys like 'order_by' are always removed from the active filters dictionary even when an explicit override value is provided.
Run the test suite to verify that solver retrieval produces reproducible results without modifying instance defaults.
pitfalls: Performing a shallow copy instead of copy.deepcopy when default configurations contain nested dictionary structures.
Forgetting to remove non-filter keys (like order_by) from filters when an explicit override is supplied, passing unsupported filter keys to the solver matcher.

kel.goal: Make Client.close() robustly prevent client component reuse
kel.desc:
Robust `Client.close()`, no client/solver/future reuse after close
After `Client.close()`:
- all workers have to be killed, immediately if user doesn't want to wait for results (which they are now too, but in a blocking manner)
- all solvers have to be invalidated, so no future submissions are possible (channel is closed),
- all futures have to be resolved (with timeout/shutdown error if `Client.close(wait=False)`)
kel.procedure: preventing client component reuse after close using weak references and state flags
steps: Identify the client and solver classes where submission, polling, loading, and background executors are managed.
Define a dedicated exception (e.g., UseAfterCloseError) for operations attempted after client shutdown.

Add an initialization flag to the client, reset it upon close(), make close() idempotent when uninitialized, and decorate submission, polling, loading, and upload methods to raise UseAfterCloseError if uninitialized.
Update solver references to the client to use weak references (weakref.ref) so that child solver objects do not prevent client garbage collection or resource cleanup.
Ensure all client executors explicitly wait for termination during close (shutdown(wait=True)) and queues complete safely.
Run the client test suite to verify tests pass and use-after-close is properly rejected.
pitfalls: Holding a strong reference to the client inside solvers or futures will prevent client garbage collection even when close() is called.
Failing to make close() check the initialization state can lead to repeated close calls attempting to rejoin or shut down terminated queues and executors.
Calling task_done() before requeuing tasks back into an active queue can cause race conditions during queue join.

kel.procedure: prevent unintended in-place mutation during array unit conversion and inspection

Ensure arithmetic operations on custom float/array wrapper classes preserve custom attributes and do not inadvertently mutate operands.
Ensure internal mass-weighting and normal mode property calculations operate on standard ndarrays or non-mutated arrays without modifying the instance's units.

pitfalls: Mutating `ValueArray` instances in-place within `to()` causes REPL autocompletion and inspection tools to permanently mutate object units when evaluating cached properties.

pitfalls: Placing closing-parenthesis relocation logic outside the specific wrap mode block causes it to erroneously inspect and strip closing parentheses from existing comment text in multiline imports.
Assuming `just_imports` always contains elements when splitting import strings to check for trailing commas, causing IndexError.

kel.goal: Fix multiline export sorting corruption with sort reexports option
kel.desc:
BUG: --sort-reexports don't work with multiple lines __all__
```python
import datetime

from mylib import (
    module1,
    module2,
    module3,
    module4,
)

__all__ = (
    "func1",
    "func2",
    "func3",
    "func4",
)
```

after using `isort file.py --sort-reexports`, becomes:
```python
import datetime

fro__all__ = ('func1', 'func2', 'func3', 'func4')
```
It seems to me that there is a problem with calculating the current index when using reexports in cases where we use multiline exports or add comments _to the beginning of the file_.
kel.procedure: relative stream seek and truncate for reexport rewriting
steps: Identify where reexported literal definitions like `__all__` are parsed and rewritten to the output stream.
Reproduce the corruption when running with `--sort-reexports` on multiline imports and exports.
Replace absolute character tracking (`sort_section_pointer`) with relative rollback tracking (`reexport_rollback`) based on the length of the line where reexport sorting started.

When rewriting the sorted code for a reexport, seek back by `output_stream.tell() - reexport_rollback`, reset rollback to 0, write the sorted code, and call `output_stream.truncate()` to remove any remaining stale output.
Verify that multiline imports and exports are sorted and output cleanly without overwriting earlier lines.
pitfalls: Using an accumulator for absolute stream position easily desynchronizes when previous sections are rewritten or multiline imports expand/contract.
Failing to call `output_stream.truncate()` after seeking and overwriting can leave trailing garbage characters if the newly formatted code is shorter than what was previously buffered.

kel.procedure: Preserve field order during validated assignment in Pydantic models
steps: Identify the Pydantic BaseModel's `__setattr__` method as the place where field assignment validation occurs when `validate_assignment` is enabled.
Understand that the original implementation of `__setattr__` for validated assignment might be causing dictionary reordering by popping and re-inserting the field's value from `self.__dict__`.

Modify the `__setattr__` method to create a new dictionary for validation that excludes the field being assigned, instead of directly modifying `self.__dict__` before validation. This ensures the original insertion order of fields in `self.__dict__` is preserved.
Verify that the field order is now preserved after assignment with `validate_assignment=True` by running the provided test case.
pitfalls: Attempting to fix the issue by only changing how the validated value is re-inserted, without addressing the initial removal of the field from `self.__dict__`, would likely still cause reordering.
Assuming the issue is related to Python's dictionary implementation not preserving order, when the problem is Pydantic's specific manipulation of the dictionary during assignment validation.

Design Environment Variable Support
# This is a Feature Proposal

## Description

As environment variables are an often requested feature for Serverless and AWS I want to start the design process, so we can start with implementing support for Environment Variables when they become ready at AWS at some point in the future. This is also important to make sure we capture existing use cases and our design reflects that.

There are three main use cases for Environment variables:

1. Expose Service resources created by Serverless to the lambda function (e.g. S3 bucket created as an event)
2. Expose custom data from the development team as an environment variable
3. Configure environment variables for use with our future SDK so we can do service discovery in an easy way

## Proposal for config syntax

For this first proposal I want to focus on giving users the ability to define environment variables on a provider or function level. In the future we can then add additional auto-generated Environment variables.

We will create an `environment` config parameter that allows you to set environment variables on your service or lambda function. If you set it on a provider level every function will get the environment variable. You can use the full power of the Variable system to set those parameters. Of course as those should eventually be put into the CF template you should be able to use any built-in Cloudformation functions as well (e.g. reference the ARN of a custom resource for an environment variable)

```
provider:
  environment:
    SOMEKEY: value

functions:
  hello:
    environment:
      SOMEKEY: othervalue
      otherkey: somevalue
      VARIABLEKEY: ${self:custom.variablekey}}
      S3BUCKET:
        Ref: S3Bucket
resources:
  Resources:
    S3Bucket:
      Type: "AWS::S3::Bucket"
```

Future updates will include automatically adding resources created from Events to the Environment and further automated setup features.

kel.procedure: Configure AWS Lambda asynchronous invocation destinations
steps: Understand that AWS Lambda asynchronous invocation destinations allow routing execution results to other AWS services. The issue describes an attempt to configure this using a direct CloudFormation resource `AWS::Lambda::EventInvokeConfig` which failed due to an `Update of resource type is not permitted` error.

Identify the correct way to configure Lambda asynchronous invocation destinations within the Serverless Framework, which is typically done via a dedicated configuration property under the function definition, rather than a raw CloudFormation resource.

Modify the `serverless.yml` to add a `destinations` property under the specific Lambda function's configuration. This property should contain `onSuccess` and `onFailure` sub-properties, each specifying a `destination` ARN.
Ensure that the destination ARN can reference functions within the same service or external ARNs, and that timeout settings are correctly handled.
Deploy the updated Serverless service to apply the Lambda destination configuration.
pitfalls: Attempting to define `AWS::Lambda::EventInvokeConfig` directly in the `resources` section of `serverless.yml` instead of using the framework's dedicated `destinations` property under the function definition, which leads to `Update of resource type is not permitted` errors.
Incorrectly specifying the destination ARN, leading to deployment failures or events not being routed correctly.
Not understanding that the framework abstracts the CloudFormation resource creation, and direct manipulation can conflict with its internal logic.

kel.procedure: Anchor comment detection regex to start of line in multiline JSX literals
steps: Identify where JSX text literal contents are evaluated for comment markers like '//' or '/*'.
Reproduce the issue by adding a test case containing a URL (e.g., 'https://...') or non-leading '//' inside JSX text nodes.
Update the RegExp that inspects literal node values by adding a line anchor '^' with the multiline flag 'm' (/^\s*\/(\/|\*)/m) to ensure comments are detected only at line starts.
In jsx-filename-extension rule, guard against linting mock input files where context.getFilename() equals '<text>'.

kel.goal: Disallow children or inner HTML on void DOM elements in React
kel.desc: Rule proposal: prevent some DOM elements from having children or dangerouslySetInnerHTML There are some HTML elements that are normally self-closing (e.g. `img`, `br`, `hr`). If you try to give these children, React will give you a warning like > Invariant Violation: img is a void element tag and must neither have `children` nor use `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. It would be nice to have a rule enforcing this. Bad: ``` jsx Children ``` ``` jsx ``` ``` jsx
kel.procedure: Enforce no children or inner HTML on void DOM elements
steps: Identify the list of void DOM elements that should not have children or inner HTML. This list is typically provided by the React framework itself.
Create a new ESLint rule that checks for JSX elements and `React.createElement` calls. For each, determine if the element is a void DOM element.

Within the rule, for JSX elements, report an error if a void DOM element has any `children` (e.g., `
Children
`) or if its `openingElement` has a `children` or `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` attribute.

Within the rule, for `React.createElement` calls, report an error if a void DOM element has a third argument (representing children) or if its second argument (props object) contains `children` or `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` properties.

Run the test suite to ensure the new rule correctly identifies violations and does not introduce regressions.
pitfalls: Forgetting to check both JSX element syntax and `React.createElement` call syntax for children/inner HTML.
Incorrectly identifying void DOM elements, leading to false positives or negatives.

kel.goal: Return sorted squares of a sorted integer array
kel.desc:
Day 118
Good morning! Here's your coding interview problem for today.

kel.procedure: Add sorted‑squares functions with brute and linear implementations

+package day118
+
+import (
+	"sort"
+)
+
+// SquareElementsSortedBrute returns the squared result of every element of the param.
+// Runs in O(N log N) due to sorting the results.
+func SquareElementsSortedBrute(sorted []int) []int {
+	result := make([]int, len(sorted))
+	for i := range sorted {
+		result[i] = sorted[i] * sorted[i]
+	}
+	sort.Ints(result)
+	return result
+}
+
+// SquareElementsSortedLinear returns the squared result of every element of the param.
+// Runs in O(N) due to merging two sorted lists into the result.
+func SquareElementsSortedLinear(sorted []int) []int {
+	result := make([]int, 0, len(sorted))
+	firstPositiveIndex := 0
+	for i := range sorted {
+		if sorted[i] >= 0 {
+			firstPositiveIndex = i
+			break
+		}
+	}
+	negI, posI := firstPositiveIndex-1, firstPositiveIndex
+	for {
+		if negI >= 0 && posI < len(sorted) {
+			a := sorted[negI] * sorted[negI]
+			b := sorted[posI] * sorted[posI]
+			if a < b {
+				result = append(result, a)
+				negI--
+			} else {
+				result = append(result, b)
+				posI++
+			}
+		} else if negI >= 0 {
+			result = append(result, sorted[negI]*sorted[negI])
+			negI--
+		} else if posI < len(sorted) {
+			result = append(result, sorted[posI]*sorted[posI])
+			posI++
+		} else {
+			break
+		}
+	}
+	return result
+}

kel.goal: Convert sorted array to height-balanced binary search tree
kel.desc:
Day 296
Good morning! Here's your coding interview problem for today.

This problem was asked by Etsy.

Given a sorted array, convert it into a height-balanced binary search tree.
kel.procedure: Construct height-balanced BST from sorted slice
steps: Understand the problem: create a height-balanced Binary Search Tree (BST) from a sorted array or slice. A height-balanced BST ensures that the difference in height between the left and right subtrees of any node is at most one.

Determine the algorithm: use a recursive divide-and-conquer strategy. The middle element of the sorted input becomes the root of the current subtree. The elements to its left form the left subtree, and elements to its right form the right subtree. This process is applied recursively.
Implement the base case for the recursion: if the input slice is empty, return `nil` (or the equivalent for an empty tree) as there are no nodes to form a subtree.

Implement the recursive step: calculate the middle index of the current slice. Create a new BST node with the value at this middle index. Recursively call the function with the sub-slice to the left of the middle element to build the left child, and with the sub-slice to the right of the middle element to build the right child.
Run the provided tests to ensure the implementation correctly produces a height-balanced BST from the sorted input.
pitfalls: Not handling the base case of an empty input slice, leading to infinite recursion or index out of bounds errors.
Choosing an element other than the middle as the root, which would result in a BST but not necessarily a height-balanced one.
Incorrectly slicing the array for recursive calls (e.g., including the middle element in sub-slices), leading to duplicate nodes or incorrect tree structure.

+package day296
+
+// BST is a binary search tree of integers.
+type BST struct {
+	Value       int
+	Left, Right *BST
+}
+
+// SortedSliceToBST constructs a BST from a sorted slice of ints.
+func SortedSliceToBST(sorted []int) *BST {
+	if len(sorted) == 0 {
+		return nil
+	}
+	mid := len(sorted) / 2
+	root := &BST{Value: sorted[mid]}
+	root.Left = SortedSliceToBST(sorted[:mid])
+	root.Right = SortedSliceToBST(sorted[mid+1:])
+	return root
+}

+package day228
+
+import (
+	"sort"
+	"strconv"
+	"strings"
+)
+
+// LargestPossibleInteger returns the largest possible integer
+// constructed by these given numbers.
+func LargestPossibleInteger(nums []int) int {
+	strs := make([]string, len(nums))
+	for i, num := range nums {
+		strs[i] = strconv.Itoa(num)
+	}
+	sort.Slice(strs, func(i, j int) bool {
+		first, _ := strconv.Atoi(strs[i] + strs[j])
+		second, _ := strconv.Atoi(strs[j] + strs[i])
+		return first > second
+	})
+	result, _ := strconv.Atoi(strings.Join(strs, ""))
+	return result
+}

kel.procedure: Deallocate TURN resources on zero-lifetime refresh requests
steps: Locate the TURN server's request handling logic for refresh requests, specifically the `handleRefreshRequest` function.
Analyze how allocation lifetimes are managed during a refresh. The issue suggests that allocations might not be properly released, leading to resource exhaustion.

Modify the `handleRefreshRequest` function to check the `lifetimeDuration` from the refresh request. If `lifetimeDuration` is zero, explicitly delete the corresponding allocation using the `AllocationManager`.

In `server.go`, refactor `connReadLoop` and `packetConnReadLoop` by moving the `buf := make([]byte, inboundMTU)` declaration after the `allocation.NewManager` call and its error check. This ensures the buffer is only allocated if the manager is successfully created.
Run the relevant tests to confirm that allocations are correctly refreshed and, more importantly, deleted when a zero lifetime is requested.
pitfalls: Assuming that all `REFRESH` requests extend allocation lifetime; a `REFRESH` with a zero lifetime is a deallocation request.
Failing to explicitly delete allocations when their lifetime expires or is set to zero, leading to resource leaks.
Ignoring the `lifetimeDuration` value in `REFRESH` requests and only refreshing existing allocations.

kel.procedure: Stabilize SVD `estimate_σ⁻` calculation to prevent infinite loops

issue:
Session.run finds incorrect Python 
**Describe the bug**
`session.run('python', ..., ....)` can not find the *virtual* environments python. 

**How to reproduce**
Here is my noxfile.py. The last line is the where the issue occurs.  There are **no** issues in creating a conda environment, installing conda packages, installing pip packages, and performing the pytest. I have verified it all and it completely works as expected (installing and using binaries and scripts in the virtual environment). The issue is only the last command which could only find a default python on the system (external). I have diagnosed the issue and it is explained below.

```python
import nox
import os
VENV = 'conda' if os.name == 'nt' else None
NAME = 'win' if os.name == 'nt' else 'linux'

@nox.session(
    python=['3.6', '3.7'],
    reuse_venv=True,
    venv_backend=VENV,
    name='test_' + NAME)
def test(session):
    if VENV == 'conda':
        session.conda_install('--channel=conda-forge', 'shapely')
    session.install('-e', '.[dev]')
    session.run('pytest')
    session.run('python', 'setup.py', 'sdist', 'bdist_wheel')
```

**Fix**

The issue is here:  https://github.com/theacodes/nox/blob/ac0992332a266f85152db8a5252b1fdf9818eb75/nox/command.py#L82

where `cmd` is `python` and  `path` will be to the virtual environments `Script` directory. Here is a picture of what `path` is:
![scripts](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6628085/66622663-90f41000-ebb6-11e9-93a9-80962aacd700.PNG)

As you can see there is no python here. The correct python is here:

![python](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6628085/66622736-dc0e2300-ebb6-11e9-9dd3-7237cb01bb08.PNG)


The change I performed to fix this issue is highlighted in the images. I changed this:
https://github.com/theacodes/nox/blob/ac0992332a266f85152db8a5252b1fdf9818eb75/nox/command.py#L36

to this:

```
if path:
        full_path = py.path.local.sysfind(program, paths=[path, os.path.dirname(path)])
```

Now everything works as expected. I am not sure if this is the best way to fix but it works well for me. If this is acceptable I can do a pull request if you would like.

Thanks for your great work!

kel.goal: Ensure nox sessions only use virtual environment executables
kel.desc:
`nox` uses `PATH` to find executables
This is a bit `tox`-like to suggest, so feel free to reject.

I was recently migrating my Pelican blog from a `Makefile` to a `noxfile`. I had `pelican` installed in a few of my base environments, but forgot to install it into the virtual environment. However, the sessions ran just fine because they referenced the `pelican` executable on my `${PATH}` even though none existed in the `virtualenv`.
kel.procedure: Control external executable usage in virtual environments
steps: Understand that Nox sessions can inadvertently use executables from the system PATH instead of the virtual environment, leading to non-isolated behavior.
Introduce a new configuration option, `error_on_external_run`, to control how Nox handles commands not found within the session's virtual environment.
Modify the `nox.command.run` function to detect if an executed command is external to the virtual environment and to react based on the `external` parameter.
Update `nox.sessions.Session.run` to integrate the new `error_on_external_run` global configuration and to handle sessions without virtual environments.
Adjust existing `session.run` calls in the Noxfile to explicitly allow external commands where appropriate.

issue:
Fetch mode hint is ignored when using `Paginator` 
### Bug Report

<!-- Fill in the relevant information below to help triage your issue. -->

|    Q                                        |   A
|-------------------------------------------- | --------------
| Version                                     | 2.20.0 / 3.3.0
| Previous working version                    | 2.19.8 / 3.2.3

#### Summary

This is related to issue #11128 and PR #11445.

When a `fetch=EAGER` association is filtered using `WITH`, it raises an error unless fetch mode is overridden by calling `setFetchMode(LAZY)` over the association.

This worked well after the fix in #11445.

Somehow, in 2.20.x and 3.3.x this bug returned, partially, only when using `Paginator` with `fetchJoinCollection` parameter set to `true`.

Seems like #11188 introduced this bug.


#### Current behavior

An exception is raised even when fetch mode is overridden.

#### Expected behavior

It should work the same with or without pagination.

#### How to reproduce

See test in https://github.com/aprat84/orm/tree/gh-11741

```
vendor/bin/phpunit --filter testSubselectFetchJoinWithAllowedWhenOverriddenNotEagerPaginator

There was 1 error:

1) Doctrine\Tests\ORM\Functional\EagerFetchCollectionTest::testSubselectFetchJoinWithAllowedWhenOverriddenNotEagerPaginator
Doctrine\ORM\Query\QueryException: Associations with fetch-mode=EAGER may not be using WITH conditions in "Doctrine\Tests\ORM\Functional\EagerFetchChild#owner".
```

kel.procedure: Update CNI DaemonSet mounts on container runtime change
steps: Identify the Kubernetes DaemonSet configuration responsible for the AWS VPC CNI (aws-node) and its volume mounts.
Locate the `kops` addon definition for the AWS VPC CNI (amazon-vpc-routed-eni) that generates this DaemonSet.
Modify the `updateStrategy` of the `aws-node` DaemonSet in its template to `OnDelete` to ensure pods are fully recreated when changes occur.

pitfalls: Assuming that merely changing the cluster's `containerRuntime` setting will automatically trigger a full recreation of all affected DaemonSet pods without explicit `kops` configuration for addon updates.

Not setting `NeedsRollingUpdate: "all"` for the addon, which would prevent `kops` from performing a necessary rolling update of the DaemonSet pods when the underlying configuration (like container runtime) changes.

Forgetting to change the DaemonSet's `updateStrategy` to `OnDelete`, which, even with `NeedsRollingUpdate: "all"`, might not guarantee a full recreation of pods if the default `RollingUpdate` strategy doesn't detect a change requiring a new pod.
